title: Test the scorer
description: Write tests that prove the streak bonus works, and that catch it when it doesn't.

tasks.title: Write down what should be true
tasks.body: assert total == 15 does nothing when it is true. When it is false, it stops the program with an AssertionError. A list of asserts is a test: it checks that code gives the answers you expect.
tasks.detail: Test a function by calling it with values you have worked out by hand: assert add_points(2, 3) == 5. A test that can never fail, such as assert True, checks nothing. A message after a comma explains a failure: assert lives > 0, "out of lives".

tasks.code:
# Tests for a tiny scorer
def points(guess, secret):
    if guess == secret:
        return 10
    return 0

assert points(4, 4) == 10
assert points(3, 4) == 0
print("all tests passed")
tasks.note: Both asserts are true, so the program reaches the print. If points() had a bug, an assert would stop the program, and the print would never run.

tasks.question: What would happen if the first assert said assert points(4, 4) == 5?
tasks.why: points(4, 4) is 10, so the assert is false and stops the program. The test itself was wrong here, not points(): a failing test can mean either.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: change the 10 to 5 in the first assert and read the error. Then break points() itself, by making it return 1, and see which assert notices.

The check has a function bonus(points, streak) that doubles the points when the streak is 3 or more, and otherwise returns the points unchanged. Write asserts that test bonus(). The check runs your tests on a correct bonus(), where they must all pass, and on broken versions, where at least one must fail. Do not write bonus() yourself: the check provides it.
tasks.starter: # Write asserts that test bonus(points, streak)
hints: Each test calls bonus() with values you choose, and compares the answer with one you worked out by hand: assert, the call, ==, and the answer.
Test both sides of the rule: a streak below 3, a streak of exactly 3, and one above it. Use more than one number of points too.
With other names: for a function half(n), assert half(10) == 5 checks a typical value, and assert half(0) == 0 checks an edge.

error_hints.text: A test failed on the correct bonus(). Work the answer out again by hand: is the value after == right?
bonus() takes two values: the points, then the streak.
The check provides bonus(): spell it exactly that way, and do not define or import it.
Your tests passed on a bonus() that never doubles. Add a test with a streak of 3 or more.
Your tests passed on a bonus() that only doubles from a streak of 4. Test a streak of exactly 3.
Your tests passed on a bonus() that always doubles. Test a short streak too, where the points stay the same.
Your tests passed on a broken bonus(). Try your tests with more than one number of points.

similar_example.code:
def half(n):
    return n // 2

assert half(10) == 5
assert half(0) == 0
assert half(7) == 3
print("half() passed")
similar_example.note: Tests for another function: a typical value, an edge and an odd number. Your tests are for bonus(), which the check provides.

other_ways.note: A table of cases checked in a loop. The message after the comma says which case failed.

other_ways.code:
def test_bonus():
    assert bonus(4, 1) == 4
    assert bonus(4, 3) == 8
    assert bonus(9, 10) == 18

test_bonus()
other_ways.note: Tests often live in functions whose names start with test_. Tools such as pytest find and run them for you; here you call it yourself.
